Title: Wondeful Effects of a Sympathetic Powder
Keywords: powder; strange cure; Indies; Persia; Florence; Carmelite; oriental; secret; surgeon; King James;
Transcription: ""(it was a religious Carmelite, who came from the Indies and Persia to Florence; he had also been in China, and having done many strange cures with his powder, after his arrival in Tuscany,) the Duke said he would be very glad to learn it of him; and the Carmelite answered, that it was a secret he had learnt in the oriental parts, and he thought there was not any person in Europe who knew it but himself, and it deserved not to be divulged, which could not be done if his Highness meddled with the practice of it, because he was not likely to do it with his own hand, but must trust a surgeon, or some other servent; so that in a short time divers others would come to know it as well as himself.""

Title: An Heroic Postscript to the Public, occasioned by the favourable Reception of a late Heroic Epistle to Sir William Chambers, Knight, &c. Almon
Keywords: William Chambers; Chinese gardens; Chinese courts
Notes: A poem that satirizes William Chambers. “Chinese courts” functions as shorthand for court politics—a way to suggest that what’s being imported isn’t just garden style but a whole aura of arbitrary, un-English power. Mason's China functions as a rhetorical mirror that criticizes British court fashion, spending, and political culture. The poem reveals Mason's fear of creeping despotism (often associated with the court of George III) and by anger at the men pushing Britain toward coercive policy and (soon) colonial war.
Transcription: ""With Chinese gardens, and with Chinese courts""
